notes.front: What is a test plan?
notes.back: Documentation that describes test objectives, means and schedule for achieving test coordination.
notes.explanation: The definition ties the document to coordination: it records what testing aims at, by what means, and when.
notes.example: Like a school trip itinerary that says where the class is going, how and on which days, but for testing.
notes.evidence: Documentation that describes test objectives, means and schedule for achieving test coordination.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test plan”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is a test strategy?
notes.back: A description of how to perform testing to reach test objectives under given circumstances.
notes.explanation: Its two anchors are the test objectives to be reached and the circumstances in which testing happens.
notes.example: Like a rowing club’s standing approach to training, set before any single regatta is planned.
notes.evidence: A description of how to perform testing to reach test objectives under given circumstances.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test strategy”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is a test approach?
notes.back: The manner of implementing test tasks.
notes.explanation: It is about how test tasks get done; in a test plan the syllabus places items such as test levels, test types and test techniques under it.
notes.example: Like deciding to paint a room with a roller rather than a brush: the job is the same, the way of doing it differs.
notes.evidence: The manner of implementing test tasks.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test approach”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.1, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is release planning?
notes.back: Planning for a whole product release, during which the product backlog is drawn up and revised.
notes.explanation: It is one of the two kinds of planning typical of iterative development, and it is the basis for the test approach and test plan across all iterations.
notes.example: Like drawing up a football club’s fixtures for the whole season before anyone picks next Saturday’s team.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.2 “Tester’s Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is iteration planning?
notes.back: Planning for a single iteration, up to its end, based on the work chosen for that iteration’s backlog.
notes.explanation: Its horizon is one iteration, whereas release planning looks ahead to the whole release.
notes.example: Like a coach’s plan for this week’s training sessions only, inside the long football season.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.2 “Tester’s Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are entry criteria?
notes.back: The set of conditions for officially starting a defined task.
notes.explanation: They sit at the start of a task: until the conditions hold, the task has not officially begun.
notes.example: Like a pilot’s pre-flight checklist that must be complete before the engines are started.
notes.evidence: The set of conditions for officially starting a defined task.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “entry criteria”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What are exit criteria?
notes.back: The set of conditions for officially completing a defined task.
notes.explanation: They sit at the end of a task: the task is officially complete only once the conditions hold.
notes.example: Like the list of jobs a landlord checks before signing off a tenant’s move-out as complete.
notes.evidence: The set of conditions for officially completing a defined task.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “exit criteria”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is the Definition of Ready?
notes.back: In Agile work, the entry criteria a user story has to meet before anyone starts building or testing it.
notes.explanation: It is the Agile name for entry criteria, applied to a user story.
notes.example: Like a kitchen that will not start an order until the ticket shows the table number and every dish.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.3 “Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the Definition of Done?
notes.back: The usual Agile name for exit criteria: measurable conditions the team sets for when an item is ready to release.
notes.explanation: It plays the part of exit criteria for the team’s work items.
notes.example: Like a bakery rule that a loaf may go on the shelf only once it is cooled, sliced and labelled.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.3 “Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is estimation based on ratios?
notes.back: A metrics-based estimation technique that applies “standard” ratios, drawn from the organisation’s earlier projects, to estimate test effort for a new one.
notes.explanation: The figures come from recorded project data rather than from experts’ judgement.
notes.example: Like a builder who knows from past houses how plastering time compares with bricklaying time, and plans the next house the same way.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is extrapolation, as an estimation technique?
notes.back: A metrics-based technique: measure the current project as early as possible, then project that data forward to estimate the remaining effort.
notes.explanation: It needs enough observations first, and the projection is usually made with a mathematical model.
notes.example: Like forecasting how long a jigsaw will take by timing how long the first quarter took.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Wideband Delphi?
notes.back: An iterative, expert-based estimation technique in which experts estimate separately and repeat the round until they reach consensus.
notes.explanation: The figures come from the experts’ experience, not from recorded project data.
notes.example: Like asking several surveyors, one by one, how long a roof repair will take instead of trusting just one of them.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Planning Poker?
notes.back: A card-based form of Wideband Delphi, popular in Agile teams: each estimator usually shows a numbered card for the size of the work.
notes.explanation: It keeps the repeated, expert-based estimating of Wideband Delphi.
notes.example: Like judges on a talent show holding up score cards, except the numbers are sizes of work.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is three-point estimation?
notes.back: An expert-based technique in which experts give an optimistic, a most likely and a pessimistic estimate, combined into a weighted mean.
notes.explanation: The syllabus names its advantage: the three figures also let the experts calculate a measurement error.
notes.example: Like a taxi driver saying: 20 minutes if the roads are clear, 30 most likely, 60 if the bridge is jammed.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is risk-based prioritisation of test cases?
notes.back: Letting risk analysis set the running order: the test cases aimed at the most important risks go first.
notes.explanation: It is one of the most commonly used prioritisation strategies; how risks are analysed belongs to risk management.
notes.example: Like a triage nurse in a busy casualty department seeing the most serious cases first.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.5 “Test Case Prioritization”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is coverage-based prioritisation of test cases?
notes.back: Letting coverage set the running order: the test cases that cover the most, for example the most statements, go first.
notes.explanation: Any measured coverage can drive it; statement coverage is one example.
notes.example: Like a cleaner who starts with the rooms that have the most floor space.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.5 “Test Case Prioritization”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is additional coverage prioritisation?
notes.back: A variant of coverage-based ordering: the highest-coverage test case runs first, then each next one is the test that adds the most extra coverage.
notes.explanation: Unlike plain coverage-based ordering, it counts only what each test adds to the coverage already achieved.
notes.example: Like picking a pub-quiz team: take the strongest player, then whoever knows most of what the team does not know yet.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.5 “Test Case Prioritization”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is requirements-based prioritisation of test cases?
notes.back: Letting requirement priorities, set by stakeholders, decide the running order: tests linked to the most important requirements go first.
notes.explanation: It depends on each test case being traced to the requirement it covers.
notes.example: Like a decorator who finishes first the rooms the client ranked as most important.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.5 “Test Case Prioritization”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the test pyramid?
notes.back: A graphical model of the amount of testing per level, with more at the bottom than at the top.
notes.explanation: The shape carries the message: the wide base is where most of the tests sit.
notes.example: Like a food pyramid, where the broad base shows what you should eat most of.
notes.evidence: A graphical model representing the relationship of the amount of testing per level, with more at the bottom than at the top.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test pyramid”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What are the testing quadrants?
notes.back: A model placing test types and test levels in four quadrants, formed by two dimensions of test objectives.
notes.explanation: The dimensions are supporting the team versus critiquing the product, and technology-facing versus business-facing; crossing them gives four quadrants.
notes.example: Like a map grid, where every square is fixed by one column and one row.
notes.evidence: in four quadrants, relating them to two dimensions of test objectives: supporting the product team versus critiquing the product, and technology-facing versus business-facing.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “testing quadrants”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: A test plan sets down how and when the test objectives will be reached: it documents the {{c1::means and schedule}} for achieving them.
notes.explanation: This is the purpose closest to the glossary definition of a test plan.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.1 “Purpose and Content of a Test Plan”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A test plan helps to make sure the test activities that are actually carried out {{c1::meet the criteria that were established}}.
notes.explanation: The plan links what the team does to the criteria agreed in advance.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.1 “Purpose and Content of a Test Plan”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which communication role does a test plan play?
notes.back: It tells team members and other stakeholders how testing will be run.
notes.explanation: People outside the test team can read the plan to learn how testing will run.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.1 “Purpose and Content of a Test Plan”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does a test plan show about the existing test policy and test strategy?
notes.back: That testing will follow them, or else why testing will depart from them.
notes.explanation: A deviation is allowed, but the plan has to explain it.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.1 “Purpose and Content of a Test Plan”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the syllabus, what does test planning force testers to face?
notes.back: The challenges ahead, for example schedules, people and costs, among others.
notes.explanation: The syllabus also names risks, tools and effort; planning guides the testers’ thinking about all of them.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.1 “Purpose and Content of a Test Plan”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which part of a typical test plan sets out the test scope, test objectives and test basis?
notes.back: The context of testing.
notes.explanation: These items describe the setting the testing takes place in.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.1 “Purpose and Content of a Test Plan”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which part of a typical test plan records what the test project takes for granted and what limits it?
notes.back: Assumptions and constraints.
notes.explanation: The syllabus lists them together as one item of typical test plan content.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.1 “Purpose and Content of a Test Plan”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In which part of a typical test plan would hiring and training needs appear?
notes.back: Stakeholders, alongside their roles, responsibilities and relevance to testing.
notes.explanation: The stakeholder part covers the people involved, including what they still need.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.1 “Purpose and Content of a Test Plan”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which part of a typical test plan covers how and how often people will be kept informed, and which document templates to use?
notes.back: Communication.
notes.explanation: This part fixes how information will flow during the test project.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.1 “Purpose and Content of a Test Plan”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which part of a typical test plan lists the product risks and project risks?
notes.back: The risk register.
notes.explanation: The syllabus names the risk register as its own item of test plan content.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.1 “Purpose and Content of a Test Plan”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which part of a typical test plan holds the test levels, test types, test techniques, and the entry and exit criteria?
notes.back: The test approach.
notes.explanation: In a test plan, the test approach gathers the decisions about how testing will be done.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.1 “Purpose and Content of a Test Plan”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which part of a typical test plan covers money and timing?
notes.back: Budget and schedule.
notes.explanation: The syllabus lists budget and schedule together as the last item of typical content.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.1 “Purpose and Content of a Test Plan”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In iterative development models, which two kinds of planning typically take place?
notes.back: Release planning and iteration planning.
notes.explanation: One looks ahead to the release, the other to the end of a single iteration.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.2 “Tester’s Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Release planning may involve refining larger user stories into {{c1::a set of smaller user stories}}.
notes.explanation: Breaking big stories down is part of shaping the product backlog for the release.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.2 “Tester’s Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In release planning, what do testers help to write?
notes.back: Testable user stories and their acceptance criteria.
notes.explanation: Testers take part in writing them so that each story can later be tested.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.2 “Tester’s Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which analyses do testers take part in during release planning?
notes.back: Project and quality risk analyses.
notes.explanation: In iteration planning, by contrast, testers join a detailed risk analysis of the user stories.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.2 “Tester’s Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In release planning, testers estimate the test effort associated with what?
notes.back: With the user stories.
notes.explanation: In iteration planning, by contrast, they estimate effort for the testing tasks.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.2 “Tester’s Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which decision about how testing will be done do testers make in release planning?
notes.back: They determine the test approach.
notes.explanation: Release planning is the basis for the test approach across all iterations.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.2 “Tester’s Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In release planning, what do testers plan?
notes.back: The testing for the release.
notes.explanation: The plan covers the release as a whole, not one iteration.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.2 “Tester’s Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In iteration planning, what kind of risk analysis do testers join?
notes.back: A detailed risk analysis of the user stories.
notes.explanation: At iteration level the analysis goes down to individual stories.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.2 “Tester’s Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which property of user stories do testers determine in iteration planning?
notes.back: Their testability.
notes.explanation: Testers check that each story selected for the iteration can be tested.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.2 “Tester’s Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In iteration planning, what do testers break user stories down into?
notes.back: Tasks, particularly testing tasks.
notes.explanation: Smaller tasks are what the effort estimates in iteration planning are made for.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.2 “Tester’s Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In iteration planning, testers estimate test effort for what?
notes.back: For all the testing tasks.
notes.explanation: In release planning, by contrast, they estimate effort for the user stories.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.2 “Tester’s Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which aspects of the test object do testers identify and refine in iteration planning?
notes.back: Its functional and non-functional aspects.
notes.explanation: Both kinds of aspect are worked out in detail for the coming iteration.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.2 “Tester’s Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is likely if an activity starts even though its entry criteria are not met?
notes.back: The activity is likely to prove harder, slower, costlier and riskier.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says “likely”: unmet entry criteria make trouble probable, not certain.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.3 “Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Entry criteria and exit criteria should be defined for {{c1::each test level}}.
notes.explanation: Each test level gets its own start and finish conditions.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.3 “Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What makes the entry and exit criteria of one test level differ from another’s?
notes.back: The test objectives.
notes.explanation: Criteria are set per level, and they follow what that level is trying to achieve.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.3 “Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which typical entry criterion asks whether the people, tools, environments, budget and time needed are on hand?
notes.back: Availability of resources.
notes.explanation: Test data counts among these resources too.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.3 “Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which typical entry criterion asks whether the test basis, requirements, user stories and test cases are ready?
notes.back: Availability of testware.
notes.explanation: These are work products the test activity needs before it can begin.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.3 “Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which typical entry criterion concerns how good the test object already is when testing begins?
notes.back: The initial quality level of the test object.
notes.explanation: A quick check that basic tests pass can show whether this level is reached.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.3 “Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which two kinds of typical exit criteria does the syllabus describe?
notes.back: Measures of thoroughness and binary “yes/no” criteria.
notes.explanation: One kind gives a level reached; the other is simply met or not met.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.3 “Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why does syllabus v4.0.1 no longer use the phrase “completion criteria” for the binary “yes/no” exit criteria?
notes.back: Version 4.0 used it for the yes/no kind alone, yet the glossary makes it a synonym of exit criteria; so v4.0.1 renamed that kind.
notes.explanation: The release notes list the change among the corrections, and 5.1.3 now says binary “yes/no” criteria, so “completion criteria” keeps its glossary sense of exit criteria.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, Appendix C “Release Notes”, “Corrections in the text”, p. 73; ISTQB Glossary, “exit criteria”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Using up the available {{c1::time or budget}} can in itself count as a valid exit criterion.
notes.explanation: Testing does not have to continue until every other exit criterion is met.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.3 “Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When is it acceptable to end testing because time has run out, although other exit criteria are not met?
notes.back: Once the stakeholders have weighed the risk of releasing without more testing and agreed to accept it.
notes.explanation: The decision rests with the stakeholders, who knowingly accept what is left untested.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.3 “Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What should stakeholders be told about any test effort estimate?
notes.back: That it depends on assumptions and will always carry some estimation error.
notes.explanation: The syllabus calls it important to make this clear.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How can a large test task be estimated, given that small tasks are usually estimated more accurately?
notes.back: Break it into a set of smaller tasks and estimate each of those.
notes.explanation: This uses the better accuracy of small estimates for the large task.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which two of the syllabus’s estimation techniques are metrics-based?
notes.back: Estimation based on ratios and extrapolation.
notes.explanation: Both work from measured data, either from earlier projects or from the current one.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which ratios are generally the best source for estimation based on ratios?
notes.back: The organisation’s own, for example taken from its historical data.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says “generally”: own data is the usual best choice.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When are the measurements for extrapolation taken?
notes.back: As early as possible in the current project.
notes.explanation: Extrapolation works from the current project’s own data.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: For which kind of development model does the syllabus call extrapolation very suitable?
notes.back: Iterative development models.
notes.explanation: Its data comes from measurements of the current project as it runs.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Wideband Delphi, what leads the experts to discuss their estimates?
notes.back: Estimates that deviate beyond the boundaries the group agreed.
notes.explanation: The boundaries are agreed by the group, and estimates outside them are what get discussed.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When does the Wideband Delphi process stop?
notes.back: When the experts reach consensus.
notes.explanation: The rounds repeat until the estimates agree.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In three-point estimation, what do a, m and b stand for?
notes.back: The most optimistic, the most likely and the most pessimistic estimate.
notes.explanation: The three figures span the range the experts expect.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the most popular version of three-point estimation, E = (a + {{c1::4m}} + b) / 6.
notes.explanation: The weight of 4 on the most likely value, plus 1 each for a and b, gives the divisor 6.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In three-point estimation, the measurement error (a standard deviation) is ({{c1::b − a}}) / 6.
notes.explanation: The wider the gap between the pessimistic and optimistic estimates, the larger the error.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Once test suites are assembled, what does the test execution schedule define for them?
notes.back: The order in which they are to be run.
notes.explanation: Prioritisation strategies decide that order.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.5 “Test Case Prioritization”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A higher-priority test case depends on a lower-priority one. Which must run first?
notes.back: The lower-priority test case.
notes.explanation: Dependencies can stop test cases running strictly in priority order.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.5 “Test Case Prioritization”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides priority and dependencies, what else must the order of test execution take into account?
notes.back: The availability of resources, such as test tools, test environments or people.
notes.explanation: Some resources may be available only in a specific time window.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.5 “Test Case Prioritization”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: With which two things does the test pyramid model support the team?
notes.back: Test automation and test effort allocation.
notes.explanation: By showing that each kind of test objective calls for its own level of automation, it tells the team where to put automation and effort.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.6 “Test Pyramid”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The higher the layer in the test pyramid, the {{c1::lower}} the test isolation.
notes.explanation: Tests higher up rely on more of the rest of the system, so they are less isolated from it.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.6 “Test Pyramid”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The higher the layer in the test pyramid, the {{c1::higher}} the test execution time.
notes.explanation: Top-layer tests are generally slower than those in the lower layers.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.6 “Test Pyramid”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The higher the layer in the test pyramid, the {{c1::lower}} the test granularity.
notes.explanation: Upper-layer tests each check a large piece of functionality.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.6 “Test Pyramid”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the test pyramid, what does test isolation refer to?
notes.back: How far a test stands apart from the rest of the system: the more it depends on other parts, the less isolated it is.
notes.explanation: The syllabus glosses isolation as the degree of dependency on other elements; read it as the inverse, since top-layer tests depend on most of the system and have the lowest isolation.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.6 “Test Pyramid”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does the syllabus describe the tests in the bottom layer of the test pyramid?
notes.back: Small, isolated and fast, each checking a small piece of functionality.
notes.explanation: Because each covers little, usually a lot of them are needed for reasonable coverage.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.6 “Test Pyramid”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What kind of tests does the top layer of the test pyramid represent?
notes.back: Complex, high-level, end-to-end tests.
notes.explanation: Each typically checks a large piece of functionality, so usually only a few are needed.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.6 “Test Pyramid”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which relationship in the test pyramid did syllabus v4.0.1 correct?
notes.back: Layer and isolation: the higher the layer, the lower the test isolation.
notes.explanation: The release notes list it among the corrections in the text.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, Appendix C “Release Notes”, “Corrections in the text”, p. 73
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the original test pyramid model (Cohn 2009), which layer lies between unit tests and the top layer?
notes.back: Service tests.
notes.explanation: The original model has three layers.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.6 “Test Pyramid”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the original test pyramid model (Cohn 2009), what is the top layer?
notes.back: User interface tests.
notes.explanation: Unit tests form the base and service tests the middle.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.6 “Test Pyramid”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are the three layers of the other popular test pyramid model the syllabus mentions, from the bottom?
notes.back: Unit (component) tests, integration (component integration) tests and end-to-end tests.
notes.explanation: The syllabus adds that other test levels can also be used as layers.

image.alt: A three-layer pyramid. Bottom and widest: unit (component) tests, many of them, small, isolated and fast. Middle: integration (component integration) tests. Top and narrowest: end-to-end tests, few of them, complex and slower. An arrow pointing up is labelled: lower granularity, lower isolation, longer execution time.

image.licence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.6 “Test Pyramid”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Agile software development, what do the testing quadrants group together?
notes.back: Test levels with their appropriate test types, test techniques and work products, among others.
notes.explanation: The syllabus also counts activities among the things grouped.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.7 “Testing Quadrants”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do the testing quadrants help test management?
notes.back: They set test types and levels out in one picture, so managers can check that none the lifecycle needs is missing.
notes.explanation: The picture also makes plain that some test types matter more at certain test levels than at others.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.7 “Testing Quadrants”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are the two dimensions that form the testing quadrants?
notes.back: Business facing versus technology facing, and supporting the team versus critiquing the product.
notes.explanation: Combining the two viewpoints gives the four quadrants.

image.alt: A two-by-two grid. Columns: support the team (left), critique the product (right). Rows: business facing (top), technology facing (bottom). Top left, Q2: functional tests, examples, user story tests, user experience prototypes, API testing, simulations. Top right, Q3: exploratory, usability and user acceptance testing. Bottom left, Q1: component and component integration tests. Bottom right, Q4: smoke tests and non-functional tests except usability.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from the ISTQB CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.7 “Testing Quadrants”
image.licence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.7 “Testing Quadrants”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the testing quadrants, what does it mean for tests to support the team?
notes.back: They guide the development.
notes.explanation: The opposite viewpoint is critiquing the product.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.7 “Testing Quadrants”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the testing quadrants, what does it mean for tests to critique the product?
notes.back: They measure its behaviour against the expectations.
notes.explanation: The opposite viewpoint is supporting the team.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.7 “Testing Quadrants”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which tests does quadrant 1 (technology facing, supporting the team) contain?
notes.back: Component tests and component integration tests.
notes.explanation: These are technology-facing tests that guide development.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.7 “Testing Quadrants”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How should quadrant 1 tests be run, according to the syllabus?
notes.back: Automated, and included in the continuous integration process.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says they “should” be automated, not merely that they can be.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.7 “Testing Quadrants”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What do tests in quadrant 2 (business facing, supporting the team) check, and how can they be run?
notes.back: The acceptance criteria; they can be manual or automated.
notes.explanation: Either way of running them is acceptable in this quadrant.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.7 “Testing Quadrants”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two kinds of test the syllabus places in quadrant 2?
notes.back: Any two, for example functional tests and simulations.
notes.explanation: The syllabus also lists examples, user story tests, user experience prototypes and application programming interface testing.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.7 “Testing Quadrants”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which three kinds of testing does quadrant 3 (business facing, critiquing the product) contain?
notes.back: Exploratory testing, usability testing and user acceptance testing.
notes.explanation: All three look at the product from the user’s side.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.7 “Testing Quadrants”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which tests does quadrant 4 (technology facing, critiquing the product) contain?
notes.back: Smoke tests and non-functional tests, except usability tests.
notes.explanation: Usability tests belong in quadrant 3 instead.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.7 “Testing Quadrants”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A test lead’s plan says the team will not use the organisation’s standard test tool on this project, and gives the reason. Which purpose of a test plan does this serve?
notes.back: B: showing adherence to the test policy and test strategy, or explaining a deviation.
notes.explanation: A test plan may depart from policy or strategy, but it has to explain why.
notes.choices:
A) Documenting the schedule for the test objectives
B) Showing adherence to the test policy and test strategy, or explaining a deviation
C) Recording the risk register
notes.choicesExplained: A is about timing, which the note does not cover. C would list risks, not justify departing from the organisation’s practice.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.1 “Purpose and Content of a Test Plan”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A plan states that the payment sandbox can only be used in the last two weeks of the project. Under which part of typical test plan content does this belong?
notes.back: Assumptions and constraints.
notes.explanation: The sandbox limit restricts what the test project can do and when.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.1 “Purpose and Content of a Test Plan”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A plan sets “85% statement coverage” as the condition for finishing component testing. Under which part of typical test plan content does this belong?
notes.back: The test approach.
notes.explanation: It is an exit criterion, and exit criteria sit in the test approach part of the plan.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.1 “Purpose and Content of a Test Plan”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: While shaping the backlog for the next release, a team splits a large “customer onboarding” story into five smaller ones. Which kind of planning is this?
notes.back: Release planning.
notes.explanation: Refining larger stories into smaller ones while defining the product backlog is part of release planning.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.2 “Tester’s Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team agrees which three stories go into its next two-week backlog and plans work only up to the end of those two weeks. Which kind of planning is this?
notes.back: Iteration planning.
notes.explanation: Its horizon is the end of a single iteration and its concern is the iteration backlog.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.2 “Tester’s Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester splits the story “export monthly statement” into tasks such as preparing statement data and checking the file layout. Release or iteration planning?
notes.back: Iteration planning.
notes.explanation: Breaking stories into tasks, particularly testing tasks, is a tester’s contribution to iteration planning.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.2 “Tester’s Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Before the first iteration, a tester helps decide which test levels and how much automation the whole release will use. Release or iteration planning?
notes.back: Release planning.
notes.explanation: Determining the test approach for the release is a tester’s contribution to release planning.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.2 “Tester’s Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: System testing is due to start, but the test environment will not exist until next week. Which typical entry criterion is unmet?
notes.back: Availability of resources.
notes.explanation: Test environments are among the resources an activity needs before it starts.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.3 “Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The build handed to testers crashes as soon as it opens, so even a quick check of basic functions fails. Which typical entry criterion is unmet?
notes.back: The initial quality level of the test object.
notes.explanation: The test object is not yet good enough for the activity to begin.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.3 “Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team rule says: “system testing is complete once 90% of the requirements are covered by passed tests.” Entry criterion or exit criterion?
notes.back: Exit criterion.
notes.explanation: It states what must be achieved to declare the activity complete.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.3 “Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Exit criterion: “branch coverage of at least 85%”. Measure of thoroughness or binary criterion?
notes.back: Measure of thoroughness.
notes.explanation: It sets a level of coverage to reach, not a simple yes or no.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.3 “Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Launch day arrives. Statement coverage is 70% against a planned 80%, and no more testing time is left. What must happen before testing can acceptably end?
notes.back: A: the stakeholders review and accept the risk of going live without further testing.
notes.explanation: Running out of time can end testing even with other exit criteria unmet, provided the stakeholders accept the risk.
notes.choices:
A) The stakeholders review and accept the risk of going live without further testing
B) The testers quietly lower the coverage target to 70%
C) Testing must continue until 80% is reached, whatever the date
notes.choicesExplained: B skips the stakeholders, who must accept the risk. C ignores that running out of time can be a valid exit criterion.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.3 “Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team agrees a story may enter the next iteration only once it has acceptance criteria and a size estimate. Definition of Ready or Definition of Done?
notes.back: Definition of Ready.
notes.explanation: These are entry conditions a user story must meet before work on it starts.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.3 “Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team agrees an item is releasable only after code review, passing automated tests and updated help text. Definition of Ready or Definition of Done?
notes.back: Definition of Done.
notes.explanation: These are the team’s conditions for calling an item releasable, which is what exit criteria define.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.3 “Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A manager asks a tester for one figure for testing an entire new banking platform, now. What fits the syllabus’s advice on estimation?
notes.back: B: split the work into smaller tasks, estimate those, and state the assumptions behind the total.
notes.explanation: Smaller tasks are usually estimated more accurately, and every estimate rests on assumptions.
notes.choices:
A) Give a single figure and present it as exact
B) Split the work into smaller tasks, estimate those, and state the assumptions behind the total
C) Refuse to estimate until development has finished
notes.choicesExplained: A hides the assumptions and the estimation error the syllabus says to make clear. C is not a technique; estimation predicts work before it is done.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: On past projects the development-to-test effort ratio was 5:2. The new project needs 250 person-days of development. What is the estimated test effort?
notes.back: 100 person-days.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Past projects show a development-to-test effort ratio of 5:4. The new project expects 400 person-days of development. What is the estimated test effort?
notes.back: A: 320 person-days.
notes.explanation: Divide development effort by the development share, then multiply by the test share: 400 ÷ 5 × 4.
notes.choices:
A) 320 person-days
B) 500 person-days
C) 1,600 person-days
notes.choicesExplained: B applies the ratio upside down (400 ÷ 4 × 5). C multiplies by 4 without dividing by 5.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Test effort in the last four iterations was 22, 26, 24 and 28 person-hours. Extrapolating as their average, what is the estimate for the next iteration?
notes.back: 25 person-hours.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team six iterations into a brand-new product has no earlier projects to compare with, but has measured each iteration. Which metrics-based technique fits?
notes.back: Extrapolation.
notes.explanation: It uses measurements from the current project, whereas ratios need earlier projects.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Four experts estimate a task, each alone: 10, 12, 11 and 30 days. The 30 is outside the agreed range. What happens next in Wideband Delphi?
notes.back: B: the experts discuss their estimates, then each estimates again in isolation.
notes.explanation: Out-of-range deviations trigger a discussion and a new round, repeated until consensus.
notes.choices:
A) The four figures are averaged and the process stops
B) The experts discuss their estimates, then each estimates again in isolation
C) The 30-day estimate is dropped without discussion
notes.choicesExplained: A stops before consensus is reached. C drops the out-of-range estimate, whereas Wideband Delphi has the experts discuss it.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Team members each turn over a numbered card for a story’s effort, talk about the lowest and highest cards, then show cards again. Which technique is this?
notes.back: C: Planning Poker.
notes.explanation: Numbered cards representing effort size, with repeated rounds, mark Planning Poker.
notes.choices:
A) Three-point estimation
B) Estimation based on ratios
C) Planning Poker
notes.choicesExplained: A uses optimistic, most likely and pessimistic figures, not numbered cards. B uses ratios from earlier projects.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Three-point estimation: a = 3, m = 6, b = 21 person-hours. What is E?
notes.back: 8 person-hours.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Three-point estimation: a = 2, m = 5, b = 14 person-hours. What is the estimate E?
notes.back: B: 6 person-hours.
notes.choices:
A) 7 person-hours
B) 6 person-hours
C) 5 person-hours
notes.choicesExplained: A is the plain average of the three figures, ignoring the weight on m. C simply takes the most likely value.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Three-point estimation: a = 3, m = 6, b = 21 person-hours. What is the estimate, with its measurement error?
notes.back: 8 ± 3 person-hours, i.e. between 5 and 11.
notes.explanation: The weighted mean (3 + 24 + 21) ÷ 6 = 8 gives the centre; (21 − 3) ÷ 6 = 3 gives the spread either side.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Tests “login”, “search” and “export” cover risks rated low, high and medium respectively. Using risk-based prioritisation, in what order do they run?
notes.back: A: search, export, login.
notes.explanation: Test cases covering the most important risks run first.
notes.choices:
A) search, export, login
B) login, search, export
C) login, export, search
notes.choicesExplained: B keeps the numbering, ignoring the ratings. C runs the least important risk first, the reverse of the rule.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.5 “Test Case Prioritization”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A unit has statements 1–10. Test A covers statements 1–6, B covers 1–4 and 7, C covers 7–10, D covers 5, 6 and 8. Using coverage-based prioritisation, which test runs second?
notes.back: B: test B (5 statements).
notes.explanation: Plain coverage-based ordering ranks by each test’s own coverage: A (6), B (5), C (4), D (3).
notes.choices:
A) Test C
B) Test B
C) Test D
notes.choicesExplained: A would be the second pick under additional coverage prioritisation, which counts only new statements. C covers just 3 statements, the fewest.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.5 “Test Case Prioritization”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A unit has statements 1–10. Test A covers statements 1–6, B covers 1–4 and 7, C covers 7–10, D covers 5, 6 and 8. Using additional coverage prioritisation, which test runs second?
notes.back: A: test C.
notes.explanation: A runs first with 6 statements; of the rest, C adds the most not yet covered (statements 7–10).
notes.choices:
A) Test C
B) Test B
C) Test D
notes.choicesExplained: B adds only statement 7 once A has run. D adds only statement 8.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.5 “Test Case Prioritization”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Stakeholders rank requirement R-B first, R-A second and R-C third. Test X traces to R-C, Y to R-A and Z to R-B. Using requirements-based prioritisation, what is the order?
notes.back: C: Z, Y, X.
notes.explanation: Each test takes the priority of the requirement it traces back to.
notes.choices:
A) X, Y, Z
B) Y, Z, X
C) Z, Y, X
notes.choicesExplained: A follows the test names, not the requirement ranks. B runs the second-ranked requirement’s test first.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.5 “Test Case Prioritization”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The high-priority test “pay for basket” needs a customer account, which is created by the low-priority test “register customer”. What should the execution order be?
notes.back: A: “register customer” first, then “pay for basket”.
notes.explanation: When a higher-priority test depends on a lower-priority one, the lower-priority one must run first.
notes.choices:
A) “Register customer” first, then “pay for basket”
B) “Pay for basket” first, because it has higher priority
C) Drop “register customer”, because it is low priority
notes.choicesExplained: B would run a test before the test it depends on. C removes the test the high-priority one relies on.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.5 “Test Case Prioritization”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The only load-testing lab is booked for the team on Thursday alone. Where does the load test go in the execution order?
notes.back: B: into Thursday’s window, whatever its place in the priority list.
notes.explanation: Execution order must take into account resources that are available only in a specific time window.
notes.choices:
A) At its place in the priority list, whether or not the lab is free
B) Into Thursday’s window, whatever its place in the priority list
C) Nowhere, because resource limits cancel prioritisation
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores resource availability, which the order must take into account. C goes too far: priority still orders the other tests.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.5 “Test Case Prioritization”, p. 50
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Test P calls one function with its collaborators replaced and runs in milliseconds; test Q drives a browser through a whole order. Which belongs higher in the test pyramid?
notes.back: Test Q.
notes.explanation: It is end-to-end, depends on many parts of the system and runs slower, all marks of the higher layers.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.6 “Test Pyramid”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team has 400 end-to-end tests and 25 unit tests. Does this match the test pyramid model?
notes.back: No: the model has more tests at the bottom than at the top.
notes.explanation: Here the top layer is far larger than the base.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.6 “Test Pyramid”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A test measures a web shop’s response times with 2,000 simultaneous users. Which testing quadrant?
notes.back: Quadrant 4.
notes.explanation: It is a non-functional test, and quadrant 4 holds non-functional tests other than usability.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.7 “Testing Quadrants”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Researchers watch customers try to book a table with a new app to see how easy it is. Which testing quadrant?
notes.back: Quadrant 3.
notes.explanation: Usability testing sits in quadrant 3, even though it is non-functional.

notes.front: Developers’ component tests run automatically on every commit. Which testing quadrant?
notes.back: Quadrant 1.
notes.explanation: Component tests are technology facing and support the team.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.7 “Testing Quadrants”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Tests are written straight from a user story’s acceptance criteria before the story is built. Which testing quadrant?
notes.back: Quadrant 2.
notes.explanation: User story tests that check acceptance criteria are business facing and support the team.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.7 “Testing Quadrants”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester spends a time-boxed session probing the refund flow for surprises. Which testing quadrant?
notes.back: Quadrant 3.
notes.explanation: Exploratory testing is business facing and critiques the product.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.7 “Testing Quadrants”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A test is written in business language to guide developers while they build a feature. Which two viewpoints of the testing quadrants does it combine?
notes.back: Business facing and supporting the team.
notes.explanation: That combination is quadrant 2.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.7 “Testing Quadrants”, p. 51
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do entry criteria differ from exit criteria?
notes.back: Entry criteria are preconditions for starting an activity; exit criteria are what must be achieved to call it complete.
notes.explanation: Both are set for each test level and depend on the test objectives.
notes.contrast: Entry: may we start? Exit: may we call it finished?
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.3 “Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does the Definition of Ready differ from the Definition of Done?
notes.back: Ready is the entry criteria a user story meets before work starts; Done is the exit criteria for a releasable item.
notes.explanation: They are the Agile names for entry and exit criteria.
notes.contrast: Ready: fit to start. Done: fit to release.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.3 “Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does release planning differ from iteration planning?
notes.back: Release planning looks ahead to the product’s release and the product backlog; iteration planning to the end of one iteration and its backlog.
notes.explanation: Release planning is the basis for testing across all iterations.
notes.contrast: Release: the whole release. Iteration: this iteration only.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.2 “Tester’s Contribution to Iteration and Release Planning”, p. 48
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does metrics-based estimation differ from expert-based estimation?
notes.back: Metrics-based estimation works from measured data; expert-based estimation works from experts’ experience-based estimates.
notes.explanation: Ratios and extrapolation are metrics-based; Wideband Delphi and three-point estimation are expert-based.
notes.contrast: Metrics: what the data says. Expert: what experienced people judge.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.4 “Estimation Techniques”, p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does quadrant 3 differ from quadrant 4 in the testing quadrants?
notes.back: Both critique the product; quadrant 3 is business facing and often manual, quadrant 4 technology facing and often automated.
notes.explanation: Usability tests go in quadrant 3, the other non-functional tests in quadrant 4.
notes.contrast: Quadrant 3: users’ view, often manual. Quadrant 4: technical view, often automated.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 5.1.7 “Testing Quadrants”, p. 51
